linkedin.label: SELEQT · post 01
linkedin.title: The paradox of successful doctors.
linkedin.body:
A person spends nearly 30% of their life learning how to become successful (or, as some people like to call it, RICH).

Then they spend the next 30% being too busy to understand what that success is doing to their life.

Not emotionally but Financially.

The better your career gets, the more things quietly start piling up which means more income, more responsibilities, more people depending on you and more goals.

And somehow, even more people suddenly become qualified to give you investment advice.

Now, take a doctor.

Years (decades to be more precise) of education and training.

And eventually, a career where someone else's emergency is usually more urgent than figuring out your own finances.

By the time there's room to think about money, someone has probably already sent:

"Sir, just one amazing investment opportunity. Guaranteed to change your life."

Which leaves very little time to ask:

"Am I actually handling my money well?"

That's the paradox.

Doctors make critical decisions every day, often with very little time.

And when it comes to their own money, they sometimes do what the rest of us do:

"Let's deal with that later."

The problem is, later has terrible appointment availability.

So officially coining the term "The Paradox of Successful Doctors."

#FinancialAwareness #FinancialLiteracy #DoctorsOfAhmedabad #HealthcareCommunity #Ahmedabad

linkedin.label: SELEQT · post 02
linkedin.title: Doctors are ironical.
linkedin.body:
They'll tell you:

"Don't ignore the symptoms."
"Get it checked early."
"Prevention is better than cure."

And then someone asks about their finances:

"Arre, I'm busy. I'll get to it."

But doctors know better than anyone: what you ignore today can become harder to fix tomorrow.

And money works the same way.

Inflation at even 6% can turn ₹1 lakh today into roughly ₹3.2 lakh in 20 years.

And according to a 2021 study of Indian doctors, 35 out of every 100 said they needed professional financial help. (So yes, "I'll deal with it later" is apparently a good financial strategy for the other 65.)

A small financial problem can stay small when you notice it early.

Ignore it long enough, and it can become expensive.

A doctor wouldn't wait for a condition to become critical before acting.

Maybe our finances deserve the same treatment.

Because when it comes to money, "I'll look at it when things slow down." can sometimes be the most expensive prescription.

#FinancialAwareness #FinancialLiteracy #DoctorsOfAhmedabad #Doctors #Ahmedabad

linkedin.label: SELEQT · post 03
linkedin.title: I've added a nominee, so my family is covered.
linkedin.body:
Most of us believe that. The law sees it differently.

A nominee is not an heir.

A nominee is the person your bank, fund house or insurer is allowed to hand the money to. Who that money finally belongs to is decided by your Will, and if there is no Will, by succession law.

In most cases, the nominee is only holding that money in trust for the legal heirs.

So you can have every nomination form filled in perfectly and still leave your family with a dispute.

Two things worth knowing:

Life insurance is the exception. When a spouse, child or parent is the nominee, they are beneficially entitled to the payout. That came in with a 2015 amendment.

For bank accounts, mutual funds and shares, nomination decides who receives the money. Your Will decides who owns it.

Fixing this doesn't need a lawyer or a whole weekend. It needs one afternoon:

1. List where your money actually sits. Bank accounts, mutual funds, PF, insurance, property, that old demat account nobody talks about.
2. Check who is nominated on each one. Most of us filled that column years ago and never looked at it again.
3. Write a Will. A simple one on plain paper, signed in front of two witnesses, is legally valid. No stamp paper, no registration.

In our experience, the most expensive financial mistakes are rarely about picking the wrong investment. They are about a form nobody checked.

If someone in your family is certain their nominee will inherit everything, send this to them.

And be honest, no checking: do you know who is nominated on your PF account?

linkedin.label: SELEQT · post 04
linkedin.title: Inflation is silently eating your savings.
linkedin.body:
At least that's what every third reel on your feed says.

And honestly? They're not entirely wrong.

Most of us were never taught how money works. We learnt compound interest for exams, not for life. Inflation, insurance, taxes? Figured out by trial and error, if at all.

But here's what those reels leave out:

Not understanding money isn't a crisis. It's a starting point.

Fear either freezes you or pushes you towards the first "hot tip" you see. Clarity does the opposite. It makes you calm, and then confident.

Getting there is simpler than it sounds:

- Learn one concept at a time
- Know where your money goes every month
- Ask the questions you think are "too basic"

So start now. Not because you're behind, but because the earlier you understand money, the longer that knowledge gets to compound.

Fear isn't a financial plan.

But understanding the basics is where a good plan begins.

What's one money concept you wish someone had explained to you earlier? Tell us in the comments. It might just be our next post.

#PersonalFinance #FinancialLiteracy #MoneyMindset #FinancialPlanning

linkedin.label: SELEQT · post 05
linkedin.title: Nobody actually teaches us how.
linkedin.body:
We're financially responsible from the day we start earning. Nobody actually teaches us how.

You get your first salary, and suddenly you're expected to know what to save, what to invest, how much to keep aside, what insurance you need, how inflation affects you, and whether that "amazing opportunity" your friend sent you is actually amazing.

And somehow, the default solution is: figure it out yourself.

The funny part is, the more you earn, the more important these decisions become. But earning more doesn't necessarily mean understanding money better.

Especially for people whose actual profession already takes up most of their time.

Take doctors. We expect them to keep learning throughout their careers, because medicine keeps changing. But when it comes to their finances, we somehow assume a one-time Google search and a WhatsApp recommendation should do the job.

Maybe that's why financial awareness matters.

Not because everyone needs to become an expert in finance.

But because everyone should at least understand what they're doing with the money they've worked so hard to earn.

#FinancialAwareness #FinancialLiteracy #DoctorsOfAhmedabad #HealthcareCommunity #Ahmedabad

linkedin.label: SELEQT · post 06
linkedin.title: The next employee wellness conversation should be about money.
linkedin.body:
We're talking about money.

Just 45 minutes of financial awareness.

And we're taking this conversation to the people who arguably have the least time to have it: doctors.

Introducing SELEQT's Investment Awareness Program (IAP).

A session created specifically for doctors and senior healthcare professionals to pause, ask the right questions, and understand the financial decisions that sit behind their careers, families and future.

No products. No selling.

Just a room full of professionals, one important conversation, that could make them look at their finances a little differently.

If you've got a room full of doctors who have more questions than answers, maybe it's time we gave them an hour to find some answers.

Because we believe financial awareness shouldn't be something you discover after making a financial mistake.

It should come before it.

And this is our way of starting that conversation.

SELEQT Wealth × Doctors
Investment Awareness Program 2026

outreach.label: Hospitals in Surat
outreach.meta: Outreach mail · written for SELEQT Wealth
outreach.title: The One Patient Your Doctors Never Examine
outreach.body:
Hello (name, if any),

Your doctors spend their days looking after other people's health. The one patient they rarely examine is themselves, at least when it comes to money. Long training, a late start to earning and demanding schedules leave little room for it.

Our Investment Awareness Programme (IAP) is a 45 minute session at your hospital for consultants, registrars and senior nursing staff. It works through questions like:

- At what number could you stop taking night calls?
- Does your nominee actually inherit, or does someone else?
- What would it take each month to fund a medical degree abroad in 2044?

The session is purely educational. We don't name or sell any product, advise individuals, collect contact details in the room or follow up with anyone who hasn't asked. We'd rather be useful to 50 of your staff than sell to one.

All we'd need is a room for an hour, 25 to 60 attendees and a date that suits your duty rotation. There's no cost to the hospital.

I've attached a short brief. Would you be open to a quick call this week, or could you point me to whoever handles staff training or wellness?
